tip: 'Sudah' marks a finished action and the verb itself doesn't change: 'sudah selesai' = already done.
'Mati' means dead or off, so 'matikan lampu' is literally 'deaden the lamp' – the '-kan' ending turns the state into something you do to an object.
'Ber-' verbs describe an activity: 'renang' → 'berenang' = to swim.
'Waktu' + clause = when (in the past): 'waktu saya kecil' = when I was little.
'-nya' marks a known thing: 'makanannya' = the food (we ordered). New info stays bare: 'makanan'.
Indonesian loves fronting the object: 'kuncinya ditaruh di mana?' = where was the key put?
Watch the space: 'diparkir' (one word) = is parked, but 'di depan' (two words) = in front. Glued 'di-' makes a passive verb; free-standing 'di' just marks a place.
Two passives chain smoothly: 'dicuci dan disimpan' = washed and put away. No 'they were' needed.
'Tolong' + 'di-' softens a request: 'tolong dicek' = please check it (lit. 'let it be checked').
Doubling an adjective spreads it out: 'dipotong kecil-kecil' = cut into lots of small pieces.
The doer can follow the 'di-' verb directly: 'dipinjam teman' = borrowed by a friend; 'oleh' is optional.
Habits use plain 'di-' with no tense word: 'diminum dua kali sehari' = is taken twice a day.
'Jangan' + 'di-' is a gentle prohibition: 'jangan dibuka' = don't open it. Focus stays on the thing.
'Harus' (must) sits straight on the passive verb: 'harus dibawa' = must be carried – no 'be' anywhere. 'Bisa' and 'perlu' work the same way.
'Oleh-oleh' = the souvenirs you bring people from a trip. Buying them is a real Indonesian custom.
Use 'oleh' when the doer matters: 'dipuji oleh atasan' = praised by the boss.
'Sedang' + 'di-' = is being X-ed right now: 'sedang diperbaiki' = is being repaired.
'Belum' + 'di-' = not yet X-ed: 'belum ditandatangani' = not signed yet. 'Belum', not 'tidak', means 'not yet'.
Daily routines sound natural in the passive: 'anak-anak dijemput jam satu' = the kids get picked up at one.
'Pelan-pelan' = slowly, gently (doubled adjective): 'dibangunkan pelan-pelan' = woken up gently.
'Mudik' = travel back to your hometown. A huge Indonesian tradition, especially before 'Lebaran'.
'Diadakan' comes from 'ada' (exist) – literally 'made to exist', the standard way to say an event 'is held': 'diadakan di rumah nenek' = held at grandma's house.
'Silakan' + 'di-' is a warm invitation: 'silakan diminum tehnya' = please go ahead and drink the tea.
In polite passive requests the object usually takes '-nya': 'diisi formulirnya' = fill in the form.
'Bangun' has two lives: 'bangun pagi' = wake up early; 'dibangun' = built (a building).
'Sudah ... atau belum' = yet or not yet: 'sudah dibayar atau belum?' = has it been paid yet?
'Pakai' = with/using for tools: 'dimakan pakai tangan' = eaten with your hands.
Ask the doer right after the 'di-' verb: 'diambil siapa?' = who took it? (lit. taken by whom?)
Hotel staff often speak in passives: 'mau dibersihkan sekarang?' = would you like it cleaned now?
'Yang' + 'di-' = 'the one that was ...': 'kue yang dibuat nenek' = the cake made by grandma.
